Mr. Speaker, I think perhaps
the best time for me to raise this question is at this point. Having regard to the fact that we now meet in this rather unusual period of the year for a session of parliament, I should like to ask the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) when we may expect reports from those ministers who have been abroad for the past three months on various important matters of government business.
I believe that before this session ends we should have a report from each of those ministers on the subject matter that was under discussion at the time they were abroad.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO REPORTS FROM MINISTERS RETURNING FROM ABROAD
speechtext:
It is necessary for some of those
ministers who have been abroad to return there, and I understand that the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) left this morning for Korea. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) is to leave on January 12 or 13 for a continuation of the meetings in London, and I do not know whether there will be an opportunity for the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) to make a report on what took place at the conference in Rome. The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) is not here this morning, and I understand he is otherwise engaged on matters that are not of international importance. As soon as he returns there may be an opportunity for a report in addition to that which he has already made in the house.
Of course, these matters are of great interest but for the last few sittings of the house we have been dealing with a matter of domestic concern which is also of great interest, and which is to be the topic of further discussion in the house this morning. I would hope that we could go on with that domestic matter without in any way slighting the international negotiations on which my colleagues have recently been engaged.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO REPORTS FROM MINISTERS RETURNING FROM ABROAD
speechtext:
Without extending the discussion of this subject unduly, I would
point out that while it is true we have before us a matter of extremely important domestic concern, the practice has been established of informing the house, prior to the orders of the day, about matters directly affecting particular departments where the minister has some report to make to the house, and through the house to the press and people of Canada. It does seem to me that the very fact that the Minister of National Defence left this morning suggests reasons why it would be desirable to give the house some assurance that we shall have reports from these ministers concerning the extremely important subjects they were discussing while abroad. Naturally, all of us will be pleased that the Minister of National Defence will be visiting the Canadian troops in Korea. I would point out, however, that it is a year and a half since that military operation began, and a matter of a few days might not substantially change the importance of the visit. I would have hoped that he would give us a report relating to the discussion on NATO which will be before us, and it was for that reason I asked that information be given.
Without asking for any further commitment from the Prime Minister, I would ask that consideration be given to setting aside some time which would not affect the discussion of domestic matters, when reports from these ministers could be received.

I want to support emphatically the amendment that has come from the members of the official opposition because I feel that if this bill is to go through at the present time, under the present circumstances, it is only fair that the amendment we now have before us, which purports to set up some fair trade laws and practices, should also be included and implemented for the protection of the small retail merchant who is such an important citizen, particularly in the constituency which I have the honour to represent.

In fact, there was much evidence to indicate that the type of marketing carried on under the present practice of resale price maintenance has produced a situation of lower prices than had that type of marketing been exposed to the sort of laissez-faire free enterprise techniques that seemingly have been advocated from the government benches. This has been particularly true since the price index began to rise so alarmingly within the last year. Therefore they feel they have been giving a fair deal to the consumer. If there is any suspicion that there has been exploitation, that there has been a tendency towards unfair monopolies and combines, I am sure the type of commission which members of the official opposition have recommended to maintain fair trade laws should be adequate to deal with exploitation and monopoly interests wherever they arise. Brandon (Mr. Dinsdale) will feel that I am dealing sufficiently with the arguments he has put forward in the general remarks I

Combines Investigation Act have to make about the amendment submitted by the hon. lady who represents Hamilton West (Mrs. Fairclough). I am rising at this time to state that the amendment to the amendment put forward by the hon. lady is not acceptable to the government because it would mean in fact, as I think I will be able to show to her own satisfaction, that nothing at all would be done about the problem concerning which the government feels that something is required at this time.
The effect of her amendment is to have stand the first part of the amendment moved by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Cold well):
That Bill No. 36 be not now read a second time but that it be resolved that in the opinion of this house consideration should be given to the introduction of legislation providing-
Her amendment proposes to strike out the words in the original amendment-
-that where regulation of resale price is in the public interest such regulation should be under public control instead of under private control.
And to substitute something which the hon. lady thinks is more precise, as follows: for the establishment of a fair trade commission.
That means that this bill would not now be read a second time, but that consideration would be given to some other form of legislation, and that other form would be the establishment of a fair trade commission.
I am sure the hon. member knows, as was quite clearly demonstrated by her leader in his speech on Friday in that connection, that this was attempted in 1935. The leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) quoted the paragraph of the Dominion Trade and Industry Commission Act, and stated that if hon. members would refer to what had taken place at that time they would see why great caution should be exercised in proceeding with this measure at this time. He said, as reported at page 2350 of Hansard:
In 1935 the parliament of Canada passed the Dominion Trade and Industry Commission Act which carried into legislative form many of the ideas incorporated in the fair trade laws of the United States.
The hon. member went on to say:
I assume all hon. members know that section 14-[DOT]
The section which provided for this matter.
-was declared ultra vires by the Supreme Court of Canada.
He went on:
It is important for us to remember that, when this section was enacted, an attempt was made to put into effect in Canada what are described as fair trade practices.


Further down he said:
Further on he said that if this amendment was passed all hon. members would have the opportunity of getting legal advice upon it, and he went on:
Then if it is decided there are constitutional problems involved, as I most certainly think there are, it will be possible for them to lay the foundation for some other procedure which would bring about the kind' of result that has been obtained in other cases where it has been found that some subject of general interest to the people of Canada, but which is nevertheless exclusively within provincial jurisdiction under our constitution, can be brought into general operation.
Well, the method that has been found for doing that in the cases where it was necessary has been by amendments to the constitution; but I do not think any hon. member would feel that if there is a problem to be dealt with at this time the way to do it would be to try to get an amendment to the constitution which would allow fair trade legislation to be enacted by this parliament, because of course in these cases it was decided that under its ordinary jurisdiction parliament can forbid the doing of things which parliament feels are contrary to the public interest, but cannot regulate property and civil rights. And that it is only when that is required as an incident of national defence that the exclusive jurisdiction of the provinces can be ousted and parliament can assert as its overriding right to provide for the proper defence of the country measures which would normally be within provincial jurisdiction.
I am rising at this time because a persistent effort has been made by the official opposition in the house, and by some of its supporters in the press outside the house, to suggest that the government is halfhearted about this bill; that we do not think it is a bill of much importance. That was referred to, in I think rather typical form, by the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell), when he said at page 2196 of Hansard:
I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that the bill has become a foundling. I understand a "foundling" is a child whose parents are unknown and cannot be discovered. While the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) sponsored the measure, through the speech from the throne, in dignified words, when he came to speak about it-I was going to say he blew hot and cold, but that wotild not be correct because there was no hot, he really just blew cold on it. What he said was this, as recorded at page 41 of Hansard for October 15, 1951:
". . . as regards immediate additional measures to curb inflation, while others may develop, the only one we are prepared to submit at this time is the one that will arise out of this report of the combines committee with respect to resale prices."
Then he said:
"I do not think that is going to have a, very substantial effect on the index of the cost of living."

He went on:
Having been rejected by the Prime Minister, the bill found itself on the doorstep of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson).
Well, the bill has not been rejected by the Prime Minister, nor by any of his colleagues. The bill is the government's recommendation to parliament to deal with a problem which is recognized even by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) himself, in. his speech on Friday. We see this at page 2353 of Hansard:
We recognize the fact that there are practices which should be under restraint. We recognize the fact-as it has been recognized in earlier attempts which have been made in this house to pass legislation-that there are practices which should be stopped.
That is also recognized by the government, and was recognized by the committee. The measure we are putting forward before the house is a government recommendation to put under restraint these practices which should be under restraint, and to deal with practices that should be stopped by stopping them. Then the leader of the opposition went on to say:
What I said was that I did not think at this stage we should seek to draft the bill, but rather that we should assert as a principle that we want this measure held back so there might be further inquiry, and so the advisability of having a fair trade commission-
And so on. And when the question was put to him by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low), he said:
Without in any way seeking to evade the question, may I point out, as I did in the answer I just gave to the hon. member for Peace River, that we are not putting forward a bill, and1 that we are not attempting to cross the "t's" and to dot the "i's."
Well, we are attempting, in putting forward a bill, to cross the "t's" and to dot the "i's". This subamendment is a proposal to prevent that from being done, and instead to give consideration to something which the hon. member himself and his party realize and have stated frankly is, under present conditions, within, the jurisdiction of provincial legislatures. It was held in 1935 that the prohibitive portions of section 498A of the Criminal Code were within federal jurisdiction, and constituted valid legislation.
If, as I trust this house will find, and1 this parliament will find, there are resale price maintenance practices which should be under restraint, practices which should be stopped, the only way I know of to stop them under federal jurisdiction is the way which is proposed in this bill. And, after all, what does the bill provide? Merely that there shall not be a system of price controls organized by private agreement and enforced without responsibility to this parliament, without responsibility to the government, and without responsibility to the House of Commons, by
Combines Investigation Act such coercive measures as those who provide the product, the resale price of which is fixed, choose to exercise themselves.
We think that is not good practice. We think that under present conditions there would be no warrant for attempting to interfere otherwise with the economy of the Canadian nation than by prohibiting the things that are wrong.
There has been much debate in the house about the possible effect on some 700,000 retail traders, and of the right this would give them to take, as they should, the responsibility for prices they ask their customers to pay for the merchandise they buy from them.
On the other hand it is suggested that this is not going to have much effect on the cost of living index. I still do not think it will have very much effect on the cost of living index; but I do feel that any effect it is going to have is going to be toward a reduction of some of those prices, and toward the prevention of an upward surge of prices. And that is a fact which will be appreciated by the whole of the Canadian consuming public.
When it is suggested that it will not have much effect on prices for the consumers, and in the same breath suggested that it will destroy 700,000 retail merchants, then I think one argument cancels out the other.

I think the record of the speeches made by the hon. member for Eglin-ton (Mr. Fleming) and the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) speaks for itself; and they can be interpreted by anyone who chooses to look at the record1. It was not the view of the MacQuarrie committee, and it was not the view of the committee of the house, and it is not the view of the government that, under present conditions, there is any likelihood of this injury to any substantial number of small retailers.
I made the statement the other day, and I repeat it, that if as a result of this legislation or as a result of any other condition there develops a contrary abuse, the government will consider what recommendation it should make to parliament to deal with that contrary abuse. Because that is the only jurisdiction parliament has over these matters.
Here it is recognized that there are practices that should be under restraint, and that

Combines Investigation Act there are practices which should be stopped. Well, let us put them under restraint; let us stop them. Let us stop them now, and not have this resolution, which proposes that the jurisdiction of parliament be not exercised but that consideration should be given to something over which parliament has no jurisdiction.
It may be that we have underestimated the effect that this legislation will have on the reduction of prices. If it has any substantial effect in bringing down prices, no one will be harmed by it. Well, why, then, all this opposition against it-if no one will be harmed by it? It is apparent, not from anything I have heard outside but from what I have seen from the evidence before the committee of this house, that such important bodies as the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada and the Canadian Association of Consumers expect that those who belong to those bodies will derive some benefit from this greater freedom in the retailing trade of this country.
It has been suggested for some years now that the Conservative party was the only true liberal party, the only one that wanted to free the Canadian economy from these shackles. Here we bring forward one measure, one concrete measure, to free the retail trade of Canada from the shackles imposed upon them, not by parliament, not by a public authority, but by small groups of producers of the commodities they handle. The attitude taken in face of the proposal to free these retailers from these shackles is that which we have met since the second reading of this bill was proposed.
It seems to me that the partisans of free enterprise, of that freedom of trade which is possible under world conditions, should feel that it is proper for the retail merchant, who is the merchant with whom the consumers by and large have their dealings, should take the responsibility toward the individual purchaser of the price he asks him to pay. It may be that that price will still be the price suggested by the producer of the goods, but it will be the responsibility taken by the retail vendor and not by the producer of the goods to demand it from the consumer.
There is nothing proposed in this legislation which will prevent the suggestion of what would be a fair price. One would imagine that if the price suggested is fair it is apt to be adhered to. There is nothing in this bill which would prevent a producer fixing the maximum price at which his goods could be sold. But there will be in the bill a responsibility placed upon the dealer, whoever he is, for the price which he asks his


customer, the one with whom he makes his contract, to pay for the article the purchaser wishes to acquire.
If it be true, as I think a large body of consumers in Canada feel it is at the present time, that there are practices prevalent which should be under restraint, that there are practices prevalent which should be stopped, let us deal with those at the present time. It has been suggested that there may arise other problems; but the MacQuarrie committee, the joint committee of the House of Commons and the Senate, and we on this side feel that that is not apt to happen. If it does happen, it will be time to deal with it when it does happen and in the form in which it does happen.
That is the proposal that is before the house. That is why the subamendment which the hon. lady from Hamilton West has moved cannot be accepted as an adequate solution of the problem which exists at the present time. I spoke on the amendment moved by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar and I shall not add anything on that score.
I am not in any way complaining of full discussion and deliberation in connection with this proposal. I particularly welcomed the contribution which the leader of the opposition made on Friday because, had he not done so, I would have felt that it was my duty to point out that the attempt made to deal with perhaps the obverse problem by fair trade legislation had been made and that all that survived was the prohibitory provision which became section 498A of the Criminal Code.
It is because both the Criminal Code and the Combines Investigation Act have been under fire before the courts and have both been found to be a valid exercise of the jurisdiction of this parliament that, when we came to the conclusion that in addition to the other measures we had adopted or had recommended to parliament for adoption to curb inflation there might be this further attempt, it was put in the form which it has taken in this bill.

The Prime Minister referred to the fact that on Friday I pointed out that we were asking for consideration of the setting up of a fair trade commission, and that in doing so I had said that it was not our intention to draft a bill or cross the "t's" and dot the "i's". He said quite properly that this was the responsibility of the government, and that the government accepted that responsibility. The drafting of a bill of this nature is, of course, the responsibility of the government, and that is exactly what I was pointing out. The drafting of a bill of this kind is the responsibility of the government, and it is not sufficient for the government to say that if we find this bill does great damage to the small merchants throughout this country, then we are prepared, after the damage has been done, to introduce further legislation which will seek to rectify that damage.

speechtext: If that happens does it not enhance your political position?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext:
That comment is not worthy of the member for Spadina (Mr. Croll). It would suggest that the only thought that is actuating the member for Spadina is a political one, and I would regret to make that suggestion in this chamber. We are not dealing with something that affects only a limited number of people. I wish to emphasize, what we have sought to emphasize from the beginning, that we are concerned with the effect of this legislation upon the Canadian consumer. We

believe that the Canadian consumer is the person who is going to suffer if our whole commercial and mercantile structure, built up over many years of trial and error, is upset by ill-considered legislation which has not been given that measure of examination which it should have been given, and which was indicated at the time that a joint committee of the House of Commons and the Senate of Canada was set up some time during the course of this present session.
It is the Canadian consumer who is going to suffer if, as a result of legislation which has no qualifying clause, those merchants who provide for their daily requirements are either forced to the wall, as was predicted by the hon. member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy), or find that they are unable to maintain that measure of service which has become part of our whole social practice in this country. Throughout Canada today the small merchant provides services which are very much a part of the daily life of our society and of the way in which the ordinary household throughout this country is operated.
The Prime Minister, correctly and in generous terms, has commented on what I said in this house on Friday about the nature of this problem. I must express my appreciation of his statement that he welcomed what I said about the nature of this problem as a whole. He referred to my statement that it is recognized that, under a system of agreed or maintained prices, abuses may creep in. I asserted that proposition in supporting the suggestion that consideration should be given to the setting up of a fair trade commission. What I said, however, did not go so far as to suggest support of the proposal now before us in this amendment which I find rather difficult to understand in view of the conflicting statements made by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) and the hon. member for York South.
The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar naturally spoke in support of the amendment but indicated that he saw no dangers which would preclude his voting for the bill if his amendment was not supported. I wish to refer once again to the clear and unqualified statement of the hon. member for York South that the government had given us no reasons for the haste in pressing this measure forward and that it must be recognized that, if price maintenance was prohibited in this way, the small merchant would be driven to the wall by the big businesses and the chain stores. That, at any rate, is the opinion of the hon. member for York South and it is one which has been expressed across this country.

What I sought to emphasize on Saturday and what I seek to emphasize again today, in view of the fact that the Prime Minister has referred to those remarks in explaining the position of the government in relation to the subamendment on which the vote was just taken, is that price cutting may appear to give to the consumer a temporary advantage which may prove illusory when the full impact of unrestrained price cutting is felt. The experience in this country as well as in the United States, whose economy is so similar to our own, and in Great Britain, has been that cut-throat competition, absolutely unrestrained price cutting, gives only a temporary advantage to the people who benefit from the sacrifice prices but that, in the end, it is the consumer who suffers when the small merchant goes under and great trusts and cartels are formed which take advantage of their increasing monopolies that result from legislation of this kind.
As has been pointed out by the hon. member for York South-and I hope he will forgive me if I refer on a number of occasions to what he said-if his prediction is correct what would result from this measure, which the leader of the C.C.F. party has said he is prepared to support if the amendment is defeated, is that the small merchant will go to the wall under the pressure of the big businesses and the chain stores. What we have been suggesting to this house is that any advantage that might come from that result would not be a long-term advantage and that it would be the consumers themselves who would in the end suffer from the closing down of many of the stores which now give them service and from the formation of still greater monopolies and cartels which would have even more effective control over prices than anything which has emerged so far.
As the Prime Minister has pointed out, on Friday I said that abuses can develop under agreements of this kind. For that very reason the test should be this:	Are the agreements in the public interest or are they not? That should be the test. After all, our responsibility in this house, as I understand it, regardless of party, is to find what is antisocial and what is not. We may have different ways of seeking to solve the problems that arise. We may have different ways of seeking to prevent anti-social conduct. Nevertheless, I think it may fairly be said that the members of this House of Commons throughout the years have generally given the people of Canada reason for some measure of pride in the fact that the thing which has guided their efforts has been that question: Is it anti-social? Is it contrary to the public interest? If it is, let us deal with it. But
Combines Investigation Act if it is not, let us be sure that we are not simply carried away by arguments which have an appealing sound but which may have many weak spots which have not been fully explored.
In this case we are not dealing with something that is new; in this case we are not asked to approach this problem without the experience of many years for our assistance and guidance. We know that over the years efforts have been made to prevent anti-social activities under any agreements that would be contrary to the public interest. That very principle was fully recognized when an earlier Liberal government introduced the combines investigation legislation in 1923. In that legislation there was a clear reservation that a combine or an association of businesses to fix prices, or to affect prices generally, would be regarded as an offence under the act if it was contrary to the public interest. There was no qualification. It must be contrary to the public interest; it must be anti-social. Why is that provision not included in the measure now before us? An earlier Liberal government felt it was important to recognize that where there were abuses there might also be agreements or understandings that would actually be in the public interest. This government has recognized that principle, because it has not introduced an amendment to the Combines Investigation Act to remove that condition from the present act. If that principle is unsound in relation to the amendment now before us, it is equally unsound in regard to these larger combines which could have so much greater effect on the life and on the welfare and on the living conditions of our people.
If it is not wise to put in the reservation that it must be contrary to the public interest, that it must be anti-social, if it is not wise to introduce this prohibition into any agreement of any kind in regard to prices, then, in the light of the experience in the milling combine investigation, why was there not an amendment introduced at the same time to withdraw that reservation that now is contained in the definition of a combine which creates an offence? Perhaps the minister might have had an argument there, because he might even have suggested that that was an explanation for his failing to act in that particular case which had been brought to his attention by the commissioner under the Combines Investigation Act. No; there is no suggestion that in regard to these great horizontal combines there should be any withdrawal of the reservation that it must be anti-social and contrary to the public interest. But

Combines Investigation Act when it comes to the merchant dealing with the public, the merchant who day by day is giving some measure of service to the public not included in any of the prices that are being fixed or that are settled by these agreements that I referred to, the government says: "Oh, no. It is admitted that there may be wrongdoing under agreements of this kind, and that being so we will make it impossible for anyone to have any kind of agreement, whether it is good for the public or not." That is exactly what we object to. We say: It is no new discovery of this government that there can be antisocial results of the agreements where the agreements disregard the public interest. We know that, and we have pointed out that the Conservative party took its stand on this subject some years ago, and has not varied from that position. I pointed out on Friday that the Conservative party introduced in 1935 a measure which was based on the proposition that there could be abuses, and also that there could be agreements which are in the public interest. It has been pointed out by the minister who has introduced this measure that there is a large spread in certain cases between the price charged by the manufacturer and the price charged by the merchant. I have no doubt that the figures he has given are figures taken from evidence that has been placed on record. But, Mr. Speaker, the evidence in regard to action of that kind does not end there. I have no doubt that there are cases that should be dealt with, and we should have some mechanism to deal with them, without simply having an all-embracing prohibition of the kind contemplated by this legislation, and in no way improved by the amendment now before us.
I would point out that if the minister is anxious to deal with this subject effectively, what he should do, even at this time, is to ask the government to agree with him that the measure be withdrawn and that there be a general examination of the Combines Investigation Act and general amendments that will deal with this whole problem. I point out to him something that a great many Canadians learned during the season which has just passed, and which many of us might not have regarded as being completely past if the delay in bringing down this important legislation had not brought us back here at this time. Many Canadians , discovered that it is not only under agreements of the kind mentioned that there can be a great increase in prices. I imagine that many people who were shopping during the weeks that preceded Christmas and saw some particular article that they wanted to buy for some member of their family or some friend were


very much impressed by the fact that things which they saw advertised in New York, Buffalo, Detroit or Chicago newspapers, or other newspapers in the United States, were in a number of cases selling for more than twice as much here as they would have sold for in the United States. That is not accounted for by tariff. That is not accounted for by any ordinary arrangements, and it certainly is not accounted for by the agreements which are regarded as the big bad wolf by the minister who is putting forward this particular legislation. These are cases where we might well regard the advisability of some supervising authority who may make inquiries and find out just why it is that articles, which perhaps gain their popularity by advertising, printed in the United States and coming into this country, are sold at the prices which they are able to command here under the heavy pressure of Christmas buying.
No, Mr. Speaker, the Combines Investigation Act should be regarded as one document, as one piece of legislation. What is sauce for the goose should be sauce for the gander. If it is wise that the public interest should be the test in the case of horizontal combines or horizontal agreements, then the public interest should be the test in the case of vertical agreements as well.
And that is the situation we have before us. The minister leaves the reservation in the case of the great horizontal combines, but in the case of the vertical combines or the vertical agreements, sought by the merchants themselves-according to the evidence given to the committee, while it was permitted to sit

the merchants wanted an arrangement of this kind, and they wanted some measure of price arrangement which would make it possible to have orderly marketing.
This is something that goes back into the memory of anyone now sitting in the chamber. Just a few days ago I saw reprinted some very interesting advertisements of nearly a hundred years ago. They were printed for the purpose of showing the difference in dollar prices of similar things at that time and today. I noticed that the prices were advertised by the manufacturer away back a hundred years ago, and presumbly those were the prices at which people expected to buy those things in the stores.
The Prime Minister has said, "It is quite possible that merchants may take the suggestion of the manufacturers". Oh, that opens up interesting possibilities. There are more ways than one of skinning a cat. And the Prime Minister says, "Even if this measure is passed, it is quite possible that the suggestion of the manufacturer, who is the

source of supply, may be taken by the merchant-even with the act in force."
Does the government believe that, or not? If the government believes that, then this measure is a hoax. If the government believes that, then this measure is a fraud on the people of Canada. If the government believes that, then I think we can only come to the conclusion that the Financial Post was right, and that the reason this bill is being pressed forward is so that when the January sales are announced the people will think they are the result of this half-baked bill.

No other reason has been given to the house. No other sound reason has been given. I suggested to the Prime Minister that, in the absence of any explanation from the minister who introduced the bill, we should have some explanation now as to why this bill cannot well stand over until the next regular session of parliament. The Prime Minister said-and while I may not quote his exact words, I hope he will agree that I properly interpret the text of his remarks in, this connection'-"it would mean that nothing effective would be done in relation to something which the government thinks should be dealt with now."
Well, how effective is it? The Prime Minister has told us-and in this I certainly am not interpreting his remarks inaccurately-"I do not think it is going to have much effect on the cost of living". If it is not going to have much effect on the cost of living, just what is the urgency? If this is a measure to deal with inflation, which we have been urging should be dealt with since the house met in special session in August 1950, after the outbreak of hostilities in Korea-I say if this is a measune to deal with inflation, then this measure is too little and too late.
Nothing the Prime Minister said this morning, and nothing the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) has said or will say, offered any sound foundation for the belief that this is in fact a measure designed to attack the vitally important problem of inflation and the cost of living. And yet this is the only measure, according to the Prime Minister himself, that this government proposes to bring forward during the course of this session to deal with the problem of inflation. The Prime Minister said this morning: If there are these evil practices to which I have referred, then, to use his words-and I hope, again, that I interpret correctly the context of them-let us stop them, and let tus stop them now.

Hear, hear.
Combines Investigation Act

speechtext: I hear from one of the Liberal members, "hear, hear".

Spadina is heard from again. I hear, "From all of us, hear, hear." Well, if that is so, then let us have before us a bill that stops those who are guilty of wrongdoing but does not stop those who have agreements that can be shown to be in the public interest.
Let us be sure that in stopping wrongdoing we do not prevent a service to the people, a service which has been given by many small merchants of this country, and given in a manner which has not at any time sought to prejudice the real welfare of consumers throughout this country.
The Prime Minister has also said that parliament can forbid the doing of those things which it thinks should not be done. I believe there would be a better opportunity to deal in more detail with that particular aspect of the matter at a later stage in the debate. However, I would point out that the whole idea or, shall I say, the basic consideration in the minds of hon. members in dealing with legislation which is in the realm of criminal law should be whether or not there is in fact some anti-social or criminal act with which we are dealing.
At no point in the arguments made in support of this bill has there been the slightest suggestion that there is any criminal offence in this instance. It is simply suggested that this is a commercial operation which should not be permitted. It has simply been suggested, without any real evidence to support the argument, that the consumer will benefit in some way if he is able to go into a store and know in advance the price he will have to pay for the article he wants.
Nowhere has there been a single argument put forward that could be taken reasonably as supporting evidence for the enactment of something that, in effect, is criminal law. Nowhere in the statements that have been made is there any evidence that could be received by this high court of parliament on which they could pass judgment that we are dealing with something in the nature of a criminal offence. The measure now before us is making any agreement that seeks to establish uniform and known price levels a criminal offence, whether in the public interest or not.
If this measure were enforced-of course we all have to admit that that is something which will remain to be seen because we still require evidence that the minister will enforce one part of the Combines Investigation Act any more than another-if this act



Combines Investigation Act is enforced, when it is made law-the uncertainty as to what might happen was indicated in the report itself when it reminded the Minister of Justice that section 498A was in the Criminal Code and that it should be enforced when there were infractions-we are going to get back to practices that a lot of Canadian consumers do not want. They would have to go into a store, ask the merchant the price of a particular article, and then the merchant might name one price and we would get back to the type of trading which the people of this country decided a long time ago they did not like, that is, haggling over prices and not being sure that they were getting as good a deal as somebody else.
We are simply turning back the clock one hundred years in this country if we prevent an arrangement which will assure that every Canadian consumer who goes into a particular store is going to get the particular article he or she wants without setting aside a substantial amount of time in which to haggle over the price. I am convinced that most if not all the small merchants of this country are not anxious to see a return of practices of that kind.
Nevertheless, once we get to the point where there can be no settled prices, then we must certainly get back to the point where the determination to do business on that basis may be too great to resist. We would certainly get to the point where merchants would not be able to settle their prices or do it with any measure of certainty because the prices would be sufficiently fluid that they would require to be adjusted.
May I emphasize the fact that we have indicated that there are immense advantages in competition. I must confess that I was interested to see the extent to which the members of the party immediately to our left seem to have accepted the same views that we have held for a long time on this subject. Nevertheless there are no absolute rules in any case of this kind. The fact that there can be a limit to the type of competition that is to the advantage of the public has been demonstrated by the extent to which this country, the United States and Great Britain have gone in trying to find some balance between unrestrained cut-throat competition and that rigidity of prices which would deny any of the advantages of competition.
I would remind the house that every argument we have put forward is premised on our belief that the Combines Investigation Act should be strengthened so that it will be a really effective instrument for dealing either with horizontal or with vertical combines which are contrary to the public interest. We

have asserted, and we reassert, the proposition that it is the welfare of the Canadian consumer which must be the one and overriding test, and that in any act of this kind there should be a reservation that the thing which we are prohibiting must be something that is anti-social and contrary to the public interest. We must certainly not find ourselves in the position of doing something that is contrary to the public interest in an effort to cure abuses by undue haste in introducing legislation to deal with abuses which we recognize can take place under agreements where prices are fixed either by the government, by individuals or by corporations in this country.
I suggest that the Prime Minister has given the strongest reasons why this legislation should stand over until next session; why this legislation should be given further consideration; why a committee of both houses should be set up which will really be permitted to inquire and to report upon evidence that is comprehensive and inclusive and not simply be a sham, as was the committee which met during the course of this session.
Those reasons are contained in the statement of the Prime Minister that he does not believe that this measure can have much effect on the cost of living. I wish to add to that the remark he did make that possibly it might have more effect than the government thinks it is going to have. That indeed would be a surprising way to act, to introduce legislation and to draw up a bill they did not think was going to have the desired effect, then introduce it and pass it just on the possibility that it may not do too much harm and may do more good than they themselves think it is going to do at this particular time. That would be a new process of legislating, and a very dangerous one indeed, if it is possible that it is going to do more good than they think, it is equally possible that it is going to do a great deal more harm.
It does of course introduce a certain excitement into life that has not ordinarily been the anticipated purpose of legislation put forward seriously by the government to this high court of parliament. The very fact that the Prime Minister, on the one hand, has said that he does not think it is going to have much effect on the cost of living and, on the other hand, that it may have more effect than they think it is going to have, suggests added reasons why in the interests of the Canadian consumer our general mercantile system should not be taken by the scruff of the neck and told that they must abandon practices that have been built up

over the years without the slightest opportunity to demonstrate that what they are doing is actually in the public interest and to the benefit of the consumer.
What has been said this morning is an added reason why this legislation should stand over until the next session of parliament so that there may be a full and comprehensive inquiry, and so that when the government does present the bill to amend the Combines Investigation Act it will be able to do what it cannot do this morning, to say that this is what we think the result will be and we give you the evidence why it will actually help Canadian consumers.

The only reasons that could possibly bring us here would be if there was urgency. I listened with care to the Prime Minister when he spoke this morning-I am sorry I have not had the chance to read his speech since then-but I do not think he made much of a case for urgency. It seems to me that he could not make much of a case for urgency when all that he could find to say about this measure which we are here to pass was that he thought it might do a bit of good; and if it was able to do any good, we ought to have it. I am not so sure that I would not agree with that remark up to a point and before I sit down I want to try to say something on that score. I hope at any rate I will make people believe that I am sincere when I say that if anyone were able to make me believe that this bill would bring down the cost of living, I would vote for it and advocate it. But as X say-and I shall try to say a little bit more about this in a minute-nothing that happened in that committee provides any evidence to that end. As a matter of fact, while the committee was not allowed to have enough evidence as distinct from opinion in order to reach a conclusion on anything, I would say that the balance of evidence was in favour of the argument that resale price maintenance actually kept costs down. Let me say this in passing because really there is a suggestion-I am sorry to say the Prime Minister used the word this morning-of wrongdoing. I will come to that matter a little bit later on. We are getting very near the stage, as the hon. member for St. James (Mr. Beaudry) pointed out the other night, where we are arraigning, we are putting in the dock -some of us are-a whole group of people, and really charging them with being a lot of profiteers, without a word of evidence. I will come back to that a little later too.
On this question of urgency I want to read a word or two. I read it the other day, but I want to bring it back here today because it is relevant and it is important, and it has never been answered. These are the words of Senator Lambert, in which he said in effect that the committee was not being allowed to do what it was set up to do. I will read his own words so there will be no danger of a wrong paraphrase. At page 248 he said:
I do not suggest that this committee should undertake as wide and as detailed an inquiry as the Curtis commission did, but I do submit that the MacQuarrie report does not begin to approach, and I do not think their investigation has begun to approach, from the public point of view, and from


the point of view of a democratic interest in this whole subject, the work that was done by the Curtis commission. The MacQuarrie report is a very well stated summary; someone has compared it to an obiter dictum of the supreme court on arguments, and I think that is what it is. There is not a word of evidence given in it. There is a summary cf arguments, pro and con, on this subject, but, to my way of thinking, it is something that invites me, as a member of parliament, to reflect back to the people of this country public opinion, to which I am responsible, some degree of evidence to support the conclusions of the MacQuarrie report.
Here we are, Mr. Speaker, being asked to act without evidence, as the hon. senator says, who was once a high official in the Liberal party, and who is respected quite apart from that-I will not say in spite of that-and his statement has not been answered, and I submit it cannot be answered successfully. Yet, the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll) says that we are guilty of obstruction because we say: Let us have the evidence. We are going to create a crime; we are going to establish a new crime, which is going to turn a lot of people into criminals unless they alter their way of doing business. We are doing that without having the evidence. How a great lawyer like the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) can reconcile that with his background, I do not know.
What is the urgency? There has been no real suggestion of urgency. The only urgency which we all feel-and I imagine it is not confined to our side of the house, though it is only on this side of the house that it will be expressed-the real urgency is the need of the government to meet the indignation and rising disturbance of mind about the high cost of living. The government is terribly anxious to do something, or to look like doing something, and of course they will be clever in making it appear they have done something. No one denies their cleverness. Indeed they will be clever at making it look as if it is going to be of great help to the consumer; and if-as we all hope and expect, or at any rate all hope-there is a little let-down in prices, why of course we will have the propaganda machine up and down the country saying that this is what did it. Whether anyone believes it or not, that is another matter.
Let us look for a little while at the merits of this measure. It was first of all put forward as a measure against inflation; but I submit that that has been practically forgotten. The Prime Minister again stated his view on that this morning, and I shall not take the time of the house to go over it. But, as the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) has already said, no one could describe it as warmer than lukewarm. The

Prime Minister was very frank and fair in what he said-I mean as to the great merits, to put it mildly, of any expectation he had. Indeed, he went further than that and he practically said: We do not know what will happen; we will try, and hope for the best.
What about the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson)? I have gone through the minister's speech. I will not pretend I read every word because it was a long speech, but I have not been able to find in there any serious argument in favour of this bill as an antiinflation measure. I hesitate to say there is no reference to it, but I have found practically nothing. Certainly, there is no serious attempt to make the suggestion that this is going to affect the cost of living, which is what it was set up for. There will of course be every effort to try to put that across to the people.
Now, what about the merits of this thing? We have to get away from the inflation side and we have to regard it purely on its merits as a reform which is to be brought into the conduct of business. We are in a rather unusual position here. I hope I shall not be saying anything improper because the Prime Minister after all has spoken on this. I hope I will not be saying anything improper if I say that I think that much the most effective speeches made outside the ranks of this party in opposing this measure were made by the hon. member for St. James and the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Gibson). Now, I would be ready to take a chance if, for example, this matter had to be referred let us say to the supreme court-I would be almost prepared to take a chance on letting it go on the speeches pro and con made within the four corners of the Liberal party. When I say "the four corners of the Liberal party" I am including the hon. member for Comox-Alberni within them for the moment. Perhaps I do him an injustice, but at any rate I think I have made my point clear.
I come to the Prime Minister because he used one or two phrases this morning that astonished me. They would have astonished me in any event, but they astonished me as coming from a great lawyer accustomed to weighing his words and accustomed to the accurate use of language. He said something like this. He referred to "recognized practices which should be under restraint". I think these were the words: "recognized practices which should be under restraint." I ask, what evidence is there of that? Let us look at the people who have taken a part in this. First of all I want to look at what one might call the principle of the thing, and I am going to read again briefly from
Combines Investigation Act what was said by Mr. Justice Brandeis, because he was a great judge, who looked at this thing from the point of view not only of common sense but of law.
As I hear some of the things that are said I wonder whether the people are bearing in mind, when they use these critical words, that they are speaking about practices which have been legal and valid and regarded as not only legal but morally right. I wonder whether they are bearing in mind that they are speaking of practices which have the sanction of law, the specific sanction of statute law, in 45 out of the 48 states. I wonder whether they are bearing in mind that there is a report, and a very able report, from Britain, a report of the committee on resale price maintenance. Again, without reading at length from it I do want to read one or two things, because I say you would have thought that the consumer was the subject of a virtual conspiracy; that he was being rooked right and left; that this was clear and recognized, and that the only thing that remained to be done was to right a great wrong. Let me read briefly, Mr. Speaker, from this report composed by able men after long investigation. I shall read from page 4. They say:
The representatives-
I read this particularly because no one who is entitled to be out of an asylum would hesitate for one minute to vote for this if he believed it was going to have a major effect on the cost of living, if he believed it was going to right wrongs which are clearly evident. Therefore it is wise to remind ourselves that it is not merely the retailers, not merely the people who are making their living by selling, who are interested in this thing. The consumers have spoken out in no uncertain way. Let me read this from page 4, section 19:
The representatives of the various women's organizations who gave evidence before us were without exception strongly in favour of branding.
"Without exception". Does that sound as if the consumers were having a gigantic fraud or a gigantic piracy practised against them? Then I go on:
They found it convenient when shopping not to have to examine everything they bought in order to assess its quality; they had found that the containers in which branded goods are normally sold helped to keep the article in a satisfactory condition.
I could read at length from this report showing similar opinions. As I said the other day, even Mr. Henry Smith, who puts in a

Combines Investigation Act strong reservation, nevertheless goes along with this report which says:
We recommend that no action should be taken which would deprive an individual producer of the power to prescribe and enforce resale prices for goods bearing his brand.
I wish to read briefly, as I said a moment ago, from page 2199 of Hansard, where I quoted Brandeis in the book called "The Brandeis Guide to the Modern World". At page 213 of that book he says:
I think it is important that we should develop the right of producers of trademarked articles, growers as well as manufacturers, to establish by contract the price at which their products shall be sold.
And then on the same page:
The right to fix the retail selling price is not an injury but an aid to business, so far as the particular branch of business is competitive. The cry against retail price fixing is based uopn a misconception.
There is a statement of one of the ablest and most broad-minded leaders of American legal and social thought in the last quarter century. No one will deny that.
I now come to the railwaymen. I was amazed that this morning the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) appeared to include the Trades and Labour Congress as in favour of this measure. I wish therefore to read from the evidence of Mr. Bengough who, I presume, speaks for the Trades and Labour Congress, and who was anything but sold on this.' Mr. Bengough is a man who looks at things in>
a judgmatical way, and who tries to arrive at a conclusion after, not before, he knows the facts. That is what we are being asked to do today, and I think it is desirable that we should remember that. We are being asked to create a new crime without having evidence, to create a set of potential criminals without having evidence.
Here is what Mr. Wismer said, in reply to questioning by the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming):
Q. May I ask Mr. Wismer if he feels that this so-called practice of price maintenance is a detriment to or perhaps in harmony with public interest?
A. I think we can say this, in so far as the deal is made privately and enforced privately we would have to say No, but where it is a general practice I think we would have to have a lot more information.
Well, does this support this legislation? Does that sound as if the Trades and Labour Congress were supporting this legislation? They have the sense to stop, look and listen. They have the sense to say, "Let us have the facts from sound, hard-headed businessmen." Labour men approach this matter in what I think is the proper manner, whereas some skilled legislators do not.

Then I should like to read from the questioning of Mr. Bengough by the hon. member for Eglinton, as follows:
You will recall it purports to propose blanket prohibition on resale prices. Would you think that is a proper and desirable way of going about this matter, that we have blanket prohibition, or if we are going to have legislation on it should it be left to determine whether in the particular case the particular type of agreement is in the given circumstances harmful to the public interest or not?
Mr. Bengough answered, first of all, "It would have to be flexible." Then the hon. member for Eglinton said, "You wouldn't favour a general prohibition," and Mr. Ben-gough's answer was "No".
So much for Mr. Bengough. Let us see what the hon. member for St. James (Mr. Beaudry) says. The hon. member made a fairly stiff attack on the government. He has something to say too. I must say the hon. member is an interesting study. He made an able speech. One might say that he has a good drive but very little follow through. He announced that he was going to vote with his party, although he was not in favour of the legislation. Well, I suppose one must admire the iron-clad discipline, the Prussian discipline, this indicates. I suppose it has its advantages. But it would be such a relief, such excitement, if one of the hon. members on the other side of the house would not only express his views but act upon them. However, I am not the keeper of the conscience of the hon. member for St. James, and perhaps he would not want me to be.

I wish to add a word to stress what I said1 a moment ago about the fact that this practice of branded goods has been accepted by enabling legislation in forty-five out of the forty-eight states. The hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Hees) pointed that out most effectively the other day. There seemed to be the suggestion that the law which prevails in forty-five of the forty-eight states had been imposed upon the people while they were not looking, that it was not democratic and that, somehow or another, it was not what they wanted.
Indeed, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar made some rather satirical references to the way in which American legislatures and governors are sometimes elected. However that may be, if the fact was that perhaps three out of the forty-eight states had passed this legislation that argument might have some weight. But when forty-five out of the forty-eight states have passed this legislation, when it is practically unanimous, it is pretty hard to believe that in a considerable number of those forty-five states these fair trade laws do not represent what the people want, what they approve of and what they have found to be to their advantage.
As I said a moment ago, I think there is only one thing which could have justified dragging us back here and passing this legislation under the myth or the plea that it is a matter of urgency; that is evidence which would indicate, I say "evidence" advisedly, that it was going to perform-I will not say miracles because, heaven knows, the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) did not suggest miracles-but that it was going to be effective.
Anyone who will read this mass of evidence must agree that not only is there no adequate evidence to support the view on which this bill is based, but that actually the balance of evidence which was allowed to come before the committee indicated quite the contrary, that the passing of the legislation would in all probability cause injury. I am not going to Use alarmist figures about thousands and tens of thousands of retailers being destroyed, because I do not think it is necessary to do that in order to maintain the argument; but no serious person in this house -can doubt that there are tens of thousands of

No one doubts that a day is coming when prices will tend to go downward. One of the things I object to most strongly is something which has been said before in this house. I indicated the other day that no less a person than the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) seemed to picture the manufacturers as sitting in their ivory towers setting prices which the consumer had to accept. It is not merely a classroom statement, it is not merely a statement by economists, to say that in a very real sense it is the consumer who fixes the price. Anyone who knows business knows that manufacturers do not fix prices and then go off and forget about them for months. They are studying the market from day to day. They know that if the price is at level A they will sell so much. They know that if they can bring it down a little they will sell more. Of course it is in their interest, it is only common sense to be constantly trying to find a price at which they can sell the most. Is not that in the interests of the consumer? They would not live if they were not trying to serve the interests of the consumer. I am not suggesting that they do that in a sentimental or altruistic frame of mind; it is simply hard-headed common-sense business.
We are all consumers. We are all interested in prices. I do not suppose anyone imagines that when you cross this gangway the interest of the consumer is any less on this side than it is on the other. All we are asking is that we proceed with this thing in an orderly manner. We know from our own experience that it is not just a lot of theory when you talk about ruthless and destructive competition. It is within the memory of many people when the Standard Oil Company was considered to be a monopoly which had knocked out many smaller people. As a matter of fact, going back to the fears of the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll), despite all his great threats, despite all his assurances that we on this side of the house were unfortunate in not being able to keep in touch with public opinion, he did seem to be a little worried because he knew how things were going. He knew there will be this loss-leader business, that there will be attempts made by the huge distributors to impose their own brands. It will not be only the small business people

It is true the hon. member for Spadina has used some rough words which the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier) would never use, but on the other hand the Prime Minister was much softer this morning and it may be that we are not going to have closure applied.
I want to say what I said in the beginning, that I believe we in the opposition have a duty to perform. I am sure there have been many cases where oppositions have held out and the public has had time to learn. The hon. member for Spadina is ready to certify to us that the public is learning and that that is going to be injurious to us. We will have to take that chance. So far as the opposition is concerned we have a duty to perform, and I hope we will not be terrified by the hon. member for Spadina or by any other person, more or less formidable.
I should just like to repeat what I said before, that no real evidence has been given to us of any reason why this matter cannot be left over and the evidence obtained which Senator Lambert said had been denied, and which no single man would say was not necessary before legislation of this kind could be passed. There has not been a scintilla of a reason given as to why that cannot happen.
Secondly, there is no evidence, and I mean, no evidence on balance, that this law will bring down prices. The balance of evidence is that it will tend to raise prices. To ask us to agree that this measure shall be passed when there are so many reasons against it, and when none as yet has been given for it that can bear the slightest examination, is something that should not be done. I consider that we are merely doing our plain duty in asking delay in this legislation. Important as it may be, it is not of such importance that it should be hurried through. No one can suggest that anyone is going to be injured if it is left for two, three or four weeks until we meet again. On the other hand there is every reason to believe that if it is hurried through it will injure large numbers of our fellow citizens who have never had a proper chance to state their case before the committee.

That is a very dangerous method of determining what should be done. What the Prime Minister said is as definite as can be. It is a dangerous thing to apply closure. before the Christmas recess. I hope that out of what has taken place in recent days will come an end to the practice of legislation important to the welfare of millions of consumers in the country being introduced in the last days of the session, apparently in a desire to force it through regardless of any representations that might be made against it if time and opportunity were given.
I was not a member of the committee, but I have had representations made as to unfairness shown to various organizations in this country. I refer to the retail merchants of Saskatchewan, the largest organization of retail merchants in the Dominion of Canada, and allied with no other organization. The 2,400 members of this organization sent in a brief and requested the privilege of explaining it before the committee. The chairman denied them that opportunity upon the excuse that another organization had spoken for them. I find strong opposition to the manner in which the committee was conducted. Apparently it was conducted upon the basis that only the evidence of those who might be considered favourable toward the legislation would be heard, and those who would present any evidence to the contrary were denied the full opportunity of doing so.
I listened with a great deal of interest today to the words of the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll). The hon. member, who has a knowledge of business and a full realization of the dangers of this legislation, asked the committee to accept an amendment that would put a stop to loss leaders. He pointed out from the experience of the past the danger of loss leaders. To begin with they may be beneficial to the consumer, but later become detrimental to the consumer as well as the small businessman. The amendment moved by the hon. member for Spadina was turned down. Had it been accepted it would have gone a long way toward removing many of the objections taken to this legislation. Today the hon. member expressed the hope that if things turn out badly under this legislation, at the next session the government will take action. Was there any reason for the rush, the unseemly haste in connection with this legislation? If the conditions referred to by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) are in fact true, why has this government waited for sixteen years to remedy them? If conditions are as described by my hon. friends opposite, why the unseemly haste in endeavouring to cram this legislation through in the last days of the session? No one has explained that as yet.

I took the trouble to read the judgments of the United States supreme court on the subject, and in particular the judgments of one of the most anti-trust jurists the United States ever produced, one of the great philosophers on the United States supreme court, the late Mr. Justice Brandeis. He referred to this practice in these words:
The Sherman law-
That is the law against trusts.
-seeks to protect men In the right freely to compete and to prevent practices which must result in suppressing competition. It seeks to preserve to the individual both the opportunity and the incentive to create. It seeks to encourage the individual effort. The right of an individual manufacturer in a competitive business to market his goods in his own way, by fixing, if he desires, the selling price to the consumer-is in entire harmony with the underlying principle of the Sherman law.
Then Mr. Justice Brandeis said this in another judgment:
Americans should be under no illusions as to the values or effect of price cutting. It has been the most potent weapon of monopoly-a means of killing the small rival to which the great trusts have resorted most frequently. It is so simple, so effective. Farseeing organized capital secures by this means the co-operation of the shortsighted unorganized consumer to his own undoing. Thoughtless or weak, he yields to the temptation of trifling immediate gain, and, selling his birthright for a mess of pottage, becomes himself an instrument of monopoly.
Over and over again, Mr. Justice Brandeis dealt with that phase, the need to protect the consumer against the rapacity of these great businesses that, in their desire to destroy competition, resort to price cutting through loss leaders. Combines Investigation Act He had to admit that unless something was done to meet the question of loss leaders the legislation being introduced wouM be almost ineffectual, or certainly far from as effectual as it should be. Therefore I asked myself, why is it that this government does not bring in legislation to stop loss leader practices that have been proven so dangerous? Why is small business in this country to be placed in a position of jeopardy? Why is the consumer going to be placed in a position where, while enjoying a temporary advantage in prices, once competition has been removed he will ultimately be required to pay more for other products as well as the product upon which the cut is taking place? Again I make this suggestion, that we in this house redraft the combines act and make it an instrument to preserve the consumer from exploitation, while assuring to business a fair and reasonable profit. The profit line has become the danger line, the strife line. It is time some people in our country realize that unless there is a profit in business there cannot be wages for labour, nor fair prices to the primary producer. Fair and reasonable prices which ensure a fair and proper return in profits and permit an available reserve being plowed back into business in order to assure further jobs are the foundation of economic prosperity.
To sum up, in my opinion the effect of this legislation will be: First, in our desire to protect consumers we will in fact ultimately be harming them unless legislation is brought in to meet the loss-leader problem. Second, I think of many products that are the same price in Ottawa as in Saskatoon and Vancouver. That will end, under this legislation. We on the prairies and the people in the maritime provinces, who now have the advantage of having the same prices on these commodities as do the people in Ontario and Quebec, will find ourselves penalized by the discriminatory freight rates which will have to be added to the price of each commodity. And instead of the removal of price fixing on many products being advantageous to the consumer it will mean that those of us in distant parts of Canada will have to make up an amount that up to now has been included in a fixed price made applicable everywhere in our country.
This legislation as it now stands cannot carry out the will of parliament, if that be to assure a reduction in the cost of living. When I see the government playing around with a matter such as this, with prices going up at all times, I ask myself this question: Why is it that something is not being done; why is it that something was not done at this session to remove the sales tax on necessities?
