Mr. Speaker, I think we can all agree that the debate has taken a very great turn for the better today, and that to no member who has taken part in it are we more indebted for this fact than the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker), who has just taken his seat.
After having spoken at such great length concerning this matter I thought perhaps, out of some consideration for my fellow members,
I should not take any further part in the debate. However, the hon. member has raised certain points which I think require a reply, which I shall now endeavour to give.
The hon. member is always particularly effective when speaking before an audience which is not too well informed about the subject matter of his remarks. I wonder sometimes if he does not somewhat underestimate the intelligence of members in this chamber, because some of the remarks he made today are of the type one would expect to hear from him, and in a most effective manner, on the hustings where there is less likelihood of his hearers being able to check on his statements of fact and of law.
My hon. friend has undertaken to criticize the administration of the Combines Investigation Act, and this is not the first occasion upon which he has done so. I can remember that in one of the early speeches I had the honour to deliver in the House of Commons, at a time when certainly I did not have any great amount of responsibility for the administration of the Combines Investigation Act- as I was a new minister who had just come in-I undertook to defend the administration of that act over the years against the spirited attack which had been made against it by the hon. member for Lake Centre.
A man who is in public life and who administers legislation of this kind can pretty well reconcile himself from the start to having some rather strong criticism made against


him; some warranted, perhaps, but much of which I suggest is not warranted. But the civil servants who administer this act and who under legislation of this kind have very great powers-powers equalling those of the minister himself-are not able to defend themselves in the house. Therefore I think I ought to say a word or two concerning the administration of the Combines Investigation Act generally; that is to say, not only at the present time, but in the era when Mr. McGregor was in charge of the work, from the time it was first created by the Liberal party in the middle twenties.
In doing this I do not want to repeat what I said on a previous occasion. I do not wish to go one by one through the cases the combines investigation administration has prosecuted and refute case by case the libels, if that is not an improper word, made upon the effectiveness of the administration by the hon. member for Lake Centre. Because if I were to do that I would be merely repeating a speech I made in the house in the fall of 1949, I believe it was, and there would be no purpose in my indulging in that repetition.
But I think perhaps I can go to a more impartial source for a very objective appraisal of the Canadian combines investigation administration, a source which I am sure the hon. member for Lake Centre would be, or should be, the last to question. It is a source which would compare not unfavourably with himself in political partisanship because, like himself, this gentleman was a leading member of the Conservative party, not in this country but in the United Kingdom where perhaps, as this debate would indicate, they were a little less partisan and a little more objective in their approach to this question than we are accustomed to find them here. This is what the hon. gentleman, Mr. Leathers, said in a debate in the British House of Commons; and by the way he is one of the leading lights of the Conservative party over there and, incidentally, is Canadian by birth.
My right hon. and learned friend the member for Liverpool, West Derby (Sir D. Maxwell Fyfe) -
He has been described as one of the brightest mindis in the Conservative party in that country.
-wrote an excellent book on this subject about two years ago.
The subject was that of monopolies, generally.
One thing he said which struck me as eminent good sense, as is everything which the right hon. and learned gentleman says, was: "Other British dominions have passed laws against trade restraints though none are as complete or effective as the Canadian law."

And Mr. Leather's remarks continue:
I am sorry to see that my cousins in the states are being held up as paragons all the time. The Combines Investigation Act in Canada has worked extremely well. I know that my legal friends can ridicule prosecutions under the anti-trust acts of the U.S.A., and that it is easy to get up and point out anomalies and loopholes, but I do not think that is relevant. It is easy to attack monopolies in general, but it is even worse to defend them in particular. That is precisely what has been happening for many years.
And listen to this description by a Conservative in the British parliament of an attitude in this matter which has not been entirely absent from this debate.
Everybody says "It is a very bad thing, but when you come to my industry that is different."
I do not believe that it is different . . . Reference to this has been made in Lewis Ord's book "Politics and Poverty" and I will give an extract from it. He gives statistics which I think are of great interest. He points out that in 1815, which is a good starting date as being the end of the Napoleonic wars and when the industrial revolution was getting underway, that the real wage standard of living on both sides of the Atlantic was precisely equal. By 1890 it was still precisely equal, but we had progressed on both sides by 300 per cent. When we look at the graph from 1890 onwards, the thing goes wrong. In 1914, the North American real wage standard had increased to 600 per cent and' ours to only 400 per cent. By 1939, it had increased to 1,200 per cent and ours was only 800 per cent. Ever since they have continued to advance at ever-increasing rates. If we look at the graph as it is at present we see that the American real wage standard is nearly double ours. The critical date on the graph is 1890.
And again:
What happened is perfectly simple. In the 1890's Canada and the U.S.A. made their first halting steps towards making competition the law of the land. It was precisely at the same time that the managements, trade unions and politicians in this country started to preach collectivism and started to get together to curtail competition. I suggest that the two things are clearly relevant and must have some close connection. Therefore, when we are considering on both sides of industry productivity and real wage standards of living, I suggest that it is relevant to consider restrictive outlooks and collective outlooks in industry as part of that picture ... We do not need any more experience to enable us to prove precisely what trade practices restrict output and keep up prices. Everybody knows what they are.

I am out of order because I have to reply to things that he said that were out of order. He raised the question of international cartels and implied more or less of a smear as to what we had done in that respect. Let me say, as my hon. friend well knows, that the disposition of international cartels has to be an international disposition. If my hon. friend has been following the matter at all carefully, he will know that in the proceedings that have been taken by the United Nations, Canada has been in the very forefront in trying to arrive at some method by which international cartels can be controlled. In the meantime, however, we are confined in Canada to the prosecution of those acts which take place within Canada, and that we have carried out as in the flat glass and match cases and others where we secured convictions.
My hon. friend said that if this legislation passes we will have a great outburst of price cutting which will put the small retailer out of business. He said, and again I agree with him, that it is very difficult to get facts and figures from the Canadian picture which can

Combines Investigation Act be used in our reasoning about this particular subject matter. Professor Fuller, who appeared on behalf of the Canadian pharmaceutical association and who gave what in my judgment was the best brief of any that was submitted against the legislation, admitted freely under cross-examination that there was not a single fact or figure in his whole comprehensive brief, or in the two supplements attached to it, that was Canadian in origin. All the prices, all the facts, all the data came from the United States where, as I am sure the hon. member for Lake Centre will agree, they have built up a substantial amount of literature and statistics on that subject of resale price maintenance. The proponents of the fair trade laws of that country have, in the course of the years, built up a substantial amount of literature and Professor Fuller drew heavily from that source.
In the absence of any reliable data about the Canadian scene, the committee was asked to draw comparisons between things that were really, as Professor Fuller admitted, not comparable. We were asked to draw the conclusion that, because in an industry in which some of the products were price maintained and others were not price maintained, the mark-up on the free goods was higher than it was on the price maintained goods, that proved that resale price maintenance was a good thing. We all remember the book "1066 and All That" in which this subject or the other subject was said to be a good thing or a bad thing; on the basis of such proof we were asked to agree that resale price maintenance was a good thing in that vague sense. Those who have read the book will gather my meaning. In other words, such a comparison proves nothing. The only way in which a system of free competitive selling could be compared with a system of resale price maintenance is to compare the price of identical goods sold simultaneously under conditions as closely identical as possible in a jurisdiction in which resale price maintenance prevails and in an adjoining jurisdiction in which resale price maintenance does not prevail. To apply the rules of logic, if you are going to compare the benefits of this system with the benefits of that system you have to have every other factor in your comparison common to the two, in order to compare the results of one system with the results of the other system.
When you apply that method.-as Professor Fuller admitted!, the only reasonably sound method-it does not make any difference where you go for the facts and there are not too many places you can go. You can only

go to those places in the United States where there is a state in which free trade prevails, like Texas, and a contiguous state of about the same economic development in which resale price maintenance prevails, like California. You can make comparisons between Missouri and Illinois or between the District of Columbia and Maryland. In every one of those cases when the comparison is made by an independent body and not by some interested party, you find that the prices are substantially lower in the free trade state as compared to what they are in the other state. Not only is that the case, but in complete refutation of my hon. friend's theory that the only way in which the retail dealer can survive is with the crutch of resale price maintenance, you will find that the independent retailer in Texas has as great a percentage of the total retail business as he has in California. He has as great a percentage in Missouri as he has in Illinois, and so on throughout the comparisons.
We can invoke a fairly up-to-date example of that sort of thing. It is only a few months since an attempt was made by the Missouri supporters of resale price maintenance to have the system introduced! in a state which, up until that .time, had been under free trade. Here is a photostat copy of the St. Louis Star-Times for April 18, 1951. The headline reads:
Eleven to twelve per cent hike in drug prices expected under fair trade bill.
That is to say if the particular bill which was then suggested became law, there would be an eleven to twelve per cent hike in drug prices. Here are the comparisons of existing Illinois prices, that is under resale price maintenance, and St. Louis prices under free trade. There is a smudge on this, but I think it reads, American shampoo; St. Louis price 98 cents; Illinois price $1.39; Bayer Aspirin, 100, St. Louis price 49 cents; Illinois price 59 cents; Fleet's Phospho-Soda, St. Louis price 89 cents, Illinois price $1.29; Hadacol, St. Louis price $1.09, Illinois price $1.19; Pond's cream, $1.13 in St. Louis, and $1.39 in Illinois. I am happy to say, Mr. Speaker, that the attempt to secure passage of this fair trade law was unsuccessful.
I suggest that a great deal of the thinking of my hon. friends of the official opposition is a relic of the days of the Bennett government. They are still thinking in the terms of the period from 1930 to 1935, and all their fears of the effects upon the independent retailer are based upon the fears which every person had, and for good reason at that time. When I say that I want to make it clear that there is no implication that there was any

fault in government policies or anything of tha,t sort. The depression, of that time extended over more than one country. If my hon. friends of the official opposition who have shown considerable interest in a system of fair trade laws in the United States had only prosecuted their research a little further than they did, they would have discovered that the Miles case, in Which the Supreme Court of the United States said that the Sherman anti-trust law was applicable to resale price maintenance, was decided in the year 1912. The first trade law of the state of California, and that was the first one, was not passed until 1931. During this nineteen-year intervening period, the small retailers and business people in the United States were exposed to this predatory price cutting and all the other devices it was possible to bring against them. In spite of that, the supporters of fair trade in that country were not able to get any laws through the Congress of the United States to provide for fair trade.
The hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Hees) has made two speeches and has shown, if I may say so, great ingenuity in a new method of filibustering, in using on the second occasion exactly the same notes as he used on the first, so that the text is almost identical. In that way he saves a great deal of labour and carries' along his filibuster in an admirable way.

He portrayed to this house this beautiful picture of the operations of the fair trade laws in the United States where everybody was happy: the people who asked for them were happy, the consumers were happy, the governments who put them into force were re-elected, and so on. Mr. Speaker, those interested were not able to get the congress of the United States to pass any fair trade laws between 1912 and 1931. As anyone who has studied the subject knows, the fair trade laws that were then introduced-not in congress; they never succeeded in congress even then-but in the state legislatures, were a phenomenon of the depression. These American fair trade laws were produced by the same kind of thinking that our hon. friends of the official opposition bring into this parliament as a relic of the Bennett government days in their approach to this legislation now before us.
They tell us that these American fair trade laws are a great, spontaneous uprising supported by all of the people of the country; that they are highly acceptable to them and so on; but the fact is that the great majority of these state laws were put through without any public hearing, and without any adequate discussion, so much so that some of the central
Combines Investigation Act provisions in them around which the acts hinged contained a mistake; a bad misprint in the original act in California was repeated in several of the other states for quite a period of time before any person found that the error had been made.
Then with regard to the alleged great amount of support that there was for the Miller-Tydings amendment to the Sherman anti-trust law to provide that resale price agreements reached under the state laws would not come under the ban of the Sherman anti-trust law, what was the history of that amendment? It was introduced in congress and it was defeated. Its sponsors could not get it through in any other way so ingeniously, and I think one could apply a stronger adjective, so the sponsors of the amendment tacked it on as a rider to the appropriation bill of the District of Columbia in the dying hours of the session and put the President of the United States in the dilemma of either letting the amendment go through along with the appropriation bill or vetoing both and then not providing any money to meet the payrolls of the District of Columbia. That was the way in which the Miller-Tydings act came into effect; and this is the act and these are the fair trade state laws that my friend, the hon. member for Broadview, is recommending as a model upon which we should base our legislation.
A great attempt has been made, and without any accuracy whatever, by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) and others of his party to try to create the impression, by putting it on Hansard and having it go around the country to people who might not otherwise be informed as to what the facts were, that there had been an attempt on the part of the government, in connection with this legislation, to hold it over until the dying hours of the session in order that it could then be rushed through. Then the resolution setting up the joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons was moved in this house on November 2 of this year. I am going to be quite brief, but I want to express my unqualified support for the legislation. I listened with care to the lengthy speech of the Minister of Justice

(Mr. Garson), on the motion for second reading. I think he gave a very complete analysis of the present situation and made a good case for the legislation now before the house. I believe it would be to the advantage of the Canadian consumer and create a better understanding of this very complicated situation if the minister would have his speech printed. If he will do so I will put in my order now for 300 copies. When the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) spoke this morning he was of course speaking as a Liberal and therefore as a firm believer in free enterprise. I thought he was on sound ground when he said he thought it was the responsibility of the retailer so far as axing the price to the consumer is concerned.
I want to deal briefly with one aspect of this very complicated situation that is giving concern to large numbers of thoughtful people in the business and co-operative fields in various countries. I refer to the increasing percentage costs of distribution as the years go by. That fact has been noticed in Great Britain. It has been discovered in the United States, and without doubt it is a fact in Canada. In that regard I want to quote a few statements made by people well informed on this question. I refer to a statement by Mr. E. F. Schumacher which appeared in the London Observer of February 4, 1945. He said:
In both Britain and the United States distribution costs have steadily risen while production costs have fallen. Whether the consumer has got any benefit out of the increased productive effort is more than doubtful.
There is every indication that a rationalization of distribution may yield larger dividends in real wealth than any economies obtainable on the side of production. What is more, it is becoming ever more apparent that the lack of organization and coordination on the distributive side is the greatest single stumbling block on the road to increased productive efficiency.
Then Lord Woolton, who I believe is now the minister of food in the Conservative government of Great Britain, has characterized the distributive trades as one of the most expensive and luxurious factors of our national life. They are expensive not only in the large slice of the cost of living for which they account, but also in manpower.
I have one more reference. In dealing with this question the writer of this book says:
The methods of enforcement of resale price maintenance vary considerably but they all effectively prevent the efficient retailer from passing on the benefits of his own efficiency to the consumer in the form of lower prices.
He goes on to explain it. I believe the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) mentioned that point when he was speaking. I believe that is a question that will more and more
Combines Investigation Act seriously concern the governments of all countries. Anyone who has studied the question at all realizes that the percentage of cost allotted to the distribution of goods is, to some extent, spoiling the benefits of the increased production that is taking place now. It is a considerable factor in the increased price of consumer goods. In my opinion there is no question about it; governments will have to give some consideration to this problem because society cannot continue to subsidize inefficiency. Under resale price maintenance as I see it there has been some inefficiency in retailing throughout the years. I just make that point in passing.
We in this group fully appreciate the fears some retailers have about the effect of this legislation on their business. These people have carried on for years under certain business arrangements to which they have become accustomed, and from which many of them believe they have derived a certain amount of protection. It is for this reason the amendment was moved by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell). We are opposed to resale price maintenance because we do not believe prices should be fixed by manufacturers. When the member for Rosetown-Biggar had moved his amendment I was interested to notice that several members of the Progressive Conservative party looked it over very carefully. As I sat here watching them they reminded me of a group of coyotes sniffing at a baited trap; they thought something was hidden. As a matter of fact it was clear and concise, much more so than the amendment moved by the hon. member to my right. I believe that the implementation of that amendment in the federal and provincial spheres would have done a great deal to remove any legitimate fears some retailers may have.
There is no question about the attitude of the consumer of this country. If you were to meet a man on the street and say, "Are you in favour of manufacturers fixing prices?", he would say, "No". I believe that is evident from the representations made to the committee by the various groups. In my case it is evident from the correspondence I have received. I have received one letter from a wholesaler in my constituency in opposition to this legislation. There is no question about the attitude of the majority of the people, as is evident from the representations made to the committee by the trade union representatives. There is no question about the attitude of the farmers. The hon. member for Victoria, Ont., (Mr. Hodgson), speaking just prior to me, suggested that Mr. Hannam was not speaking for the farmers of Canada. Surely he has read the brief presented to the committee on behalf of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture.

Combines Investigation Act If Mr. Hannam was not speaking for the farmers of Canada I think we would have heard about it before now. I think Mr. Hannam's reputation is solid and well founded. He is known as a man who represents the people who have elected him to be head of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture.
So far as the southeastern interior of British Columbia is concerned, a few days ago I noticed in the press a report of a farmers' meeting at which there was a discussion of resale price maintenance. It was obvious that these men supported this legislation. One illustration of a part of the mechanism of resale price maintenance was brought to the attention of the members present. If a farmer finds it necessary to buy a dollar spring or some other small part, he finds that he has to buy a ten dollar assembly and other pieces which he did not require. It was brought out at the meeting that this is part of the mechanism of price maintenance. Then there was the excellent brief presented to the committee by the consumers association.
For a minute or two I should like to deal with the brief presented by the co-operative union of Canada. I have read all these briefs, and I thought the co-operative union made one or two points that are worth bringing particularly to the attention of the house. I mention this because I am personally interested in the co-operative movement. I have spent a good many years of my life as an official of a co-operative organization, and we have a very well developed co-operative movement in my constituency; a service co-operative operating busses, a fruit growers union, credit unions and so on. At page 700 of the minutes of proceedings and evidence of the joint committee of the Senate and House of Commons on combines legislation I find that paragraph 4 reads as follows:
In operating their co-operatives and developing a Canadian co-operative program, the consumers whom we represent encounter difficulties and frustration. It is obvious that consumer co-operatives cannot function successfully without free access to goods. But our experience is that we are denied this right because of our policy of supplying ourselves with goods at cost through the payment of patronage refunds.
This legislation is going to be of considerable assistance to the co-operative movement of this country, because I have personal experience, as a member and official of the co-operative organization, of the refusal of manufacturers and wholesalers to provide goods.
In the concluding paragraph I think there is something worth bringing to the attention of the house. In paragraph 11 on page 703 we find the following:
In dealing with the particular problem before your committee the interest of the consumer is paramount, and the submission is made primarily on


behalf of the hundreds of thousands of consumers who have through necessity organized to supply themselves with goods and services at cost. The members in these co-operatives believe that through the development of the co-operative movement they can, by the application of the co-operative method and the elimination of profit in the supplying of their goods, eventually solve to a great extent the problem of monopolies which is giving this committee and parliament such deep concern.
I heartily agree with this contention.
In support of this belief we would cite the case of the Swedish Co-operative Union and Wholesale Society (Kooperativa Forbundet). Beginning in the years immediately following the first world war, the Swedish wholesale, in company with other Scandinavian co-operatives, undertook a systematic attack on various cartels which were oppressing the consuming public. Most famous of their achievements was the successful entry into the electric lamp field which resulted in a saving of 5,000,000 kroner a year for the Swedish public. This was followed by similar attacks on the vegetable oil and cash register cartels, among others. In many cases these efforts were carried out in co-operation with other interested elements in the community.
And this is the short paragraph in which I am greatly interested:
In conclusion, we submit that co-operative enterprise, if allowed to develop normally, will of itself do much to combat monopolistic, restrictive trade practices and to supplement federal and provincial legislative action in this field.
I now want to say this in conclusion. I think this legislation is going to be of *advantage not only to the consumers of Canada as a whole but in particular to the co-operative movement in this country. When this legislation is passed it will be possible for the consumers of this country to do something for themselves, if increasing numbers of consumers would enlist in the cooperative movement, would support the promotion of manufacturing co-operatives, would support to a greater extent the development of wholesale co-operatives and would support to an even greater extent than they do today the development of retail co-operatives. The people themselves have in their own hands the opportunity of developing a co-operative movement that can be an effective check upon these unfair trade practices we are dealing with under this legislation. As a result of the investigation of the MacQuarrie committee, the investigation by the parliamentary committee, the debate in this house and the representations made by the cooperative union and other organizations of the people of this country, I trust that this legislation will bring a great stimulus to the co-operative movement in Canada and that, in so doing, it will provide a check by the people themselves on unfair trade practices.

As the Prime Minister knows so well, there were two cases referred first to the Supreme Court of Canada and later, in 1936, to the privy council. I should like to quote from the judgment of Chief Justice Duff. He was dealing with the arrangement for the approval of agreements in relation to prices and other arrangements of the very kind we are discussing now, along with other arrangements in industry or commerce, and he had this to say:
As to section 14, we cannot perceive any ground for holding that the enactments of this section are necessarily incidental to the exercise of any powers of the dominion in relation to the criminal law. Nor can the section, we think, be sustained as legislation in relation to the regulation of trade and commerce consistently with the passage quoted from the judgment of the judicial committee in Snider's case (1), in the reasons given in the judgment upon the reference concerning the Natural Products Marketing Act. It is to be observed that this section contemplates action by the commission and by the governor in council in respect of individual agreements which may relate to trade that is entirely local.
If confined to external trade and interprovincial trade, the section might well be competent under head No. 2 of section 91; and if the legislation were in substance concerned with such trade, incidental legislation in relation to local trade necessary in order to prevent the defeat of competent provisions might also be competent; but as it stands, we think this section is invalid.
That judgment refers to a section which would have permitted, in cases where it was

demonstrably in the public interest that such agreements should be permitted, agreements of the very nature which would be prohibited by the legislation now before us. That being so, I think the question naturally arises as to whether we should not have a great deal more information before us when we are called upon to pass a bill of this kind, when the possibility is raised that it might be ultra vires.
I do want to deal with one other aspect of this problem. There has been a very general impression that the parliament of Canada could declare almost anything a criminal offence, and that the courts were almost bound to accept the declaration by parliament that an act might be a criminal offence. I question if sufficient attention has yet been paid to the grounds upon which the privy council dealt with the margarine case as recently as earlier this year, at the time they had before them an appeal from the judgment of the Supreme Court of Canada. I submit that the case to which I have referred and Which is described as "in re a reference as to the validity of section 5(a) of the Dairy Industry Act, Revised Statutes of Canada, 1927, chapter 45. Canadian Federation of Agriculture, appellants; and Attorney General for Quebec and others, respondents" indicates that there have been very real limitations placed upon the authority of this parliament to declare any act to be a criminal act. I wish to quote from that judgment which is reported in Law Reports, Appeal Cases, 1951, 179, at pages 181 and 182, as follows:
The first main submission is that s. 5 (a) of the Dairy Industry Act is legislation in relation to "the regulation of trade and commerce" and therefore validly enacted under head 2 of s. 91 of the British North America Act, 1867. Secondly, s. 5 (a) and the appropriate penal provision in s. 10 of the act, is legislation in relation to "the criminal law" under s. 91, head 27, of the act of 1867. Thirdly, s. 5 (a) is a law in relation to a matter not coming within the classes of subjects assigned exclusively to the legislatures of the provinces, and is therefore within the residuary power conferred by the opening words of s. 91.
I pass to page 196 of the judgment of the privy council, and I should like to read into the record several paragraphs of this judgment because it seems to me they place this whole subject on a different basis. I feel that they should be before the members of this house who are called upon to pass judgment on whether or not the parliament of Canada is going to assume responsibility for a measure that may conceivably be beyond our jurisdiction. I start to quote at page 196 of the judgment of the privy council, as follows:
Their lordships' views on this branch of the case may be happily stated by a quotation from the judgments of the majority in the supreme court.

Rand, J., said (83) : "That object (i.e., the object of prohibition), as I must find it, is economic and the legislative purpose, to give trade protection to the dairy industry in the production of and sale of butter; to benefit one group of persons as against competitors in business in which, in the absence of the legislation, the latter would be free to engage in the provinces. To forbid manufacture and sale for such an end is prima facie to deal directly with the civil rights of individuals in relation to particular trade within the provinces; Shannon v. Lower Mainland Dairy Board (84). The public interest in this regulation lies obviously in the trade effects: it is annexed to the legislative subject matter and follows the latter in its allocation to the one or other legislature. But to use it as a support for the legislation in the aspect of criminal law would mean that the dominion under its authority in that field, by forbidding the manufacture or sale of particular products, could, in what it considered a sound trade policy, not only interdict a substantial part of the economic life of one section of Canada, but do so for the benefit of that of another. Whatever the scope of the regulation of interprovincial trade, it is hard to conceive of a more insidious form of encroachment on a contemporary jurisdiction. This conclusion is not in conflict with Attorney General for British Columbia v. Attorney General for Canada (85). (Section 498A of the Criminal Code.) There, the essential nature of the legislation was not the equalization of civil rights between competitors or promoting the interest of one trade as against another; it was the safeguarding of the public against the evil consequences of certain fetters upon free and equal competition. There is no like purpose here; there is nothing of a general or injurious nature to be abolished or removed; it is a matter of preferring certain local trade to others."
With these observations their lordships entirely agree, and they are fatal to counsel's second argument in support of the appeal. That argument would have had more weight if it had been possible to contend that the object of the prohibition was to exclude from Canada substances injurious to health. In support of their third argument, counsel relied principally on Russell v. Regina (86), and the recent case of Attorney General for Ontario v. Canada Temperance Federation (87), in which Russell's case (86), not for the first time, was considered and commented upon. In the latter case Viscount Simon, in delivering the judgment of the board, said (88) :
"In their lordships' opinion, the true test must be found in the real subject matter of the legislation:	If it is such that it goes beyond local or
provincial concern or interests and must from its inherent nature be the concern of the dominion as a whole (as, for example, in the Aeronautics case (89) and the Radio case (90)), then it will fall within the competence of the dominion parliament as a matter affecting the peace, order and good government of Canada, though it may in another aspect touch on matters specially reserved to the provincial legislatures. War and pestilence, no doubt, are instances: so, too, may be the drink or drug traffic, or the carrying of arms.
In Russell v. Regina (86), Sir Montague Smith gave as an instance of valid dominion legislation a law which prohibited or restricted the sale or exposure of cattle having a contagious disease. Nor is the validity of the legislation, when due to its inherent nature, affected because there may still be room for enactments by a provincial legislature dealing with an aspect of the same subject in so far as it specially affects that province." This passage must, however, be considered with the words used by Lord Atkin when delivering the judgment of the board in the Labour conventions case (91): "But the validity of the legislation under the general words of section 91 was sought to be established not in relation to the treaty-making
Combines Investigation Act power alone, but also as being concerned with matters of such general importance as to have attained 'such dimensions as to affect' the body politic, and to have 'ceased to be merely local or provincial', and to have 'become a matter of national concern'. It is interesting to notice how often the words used by Lord Watson in Attorney-General for Ontario v. Attorney-General for the dominion (92) have unsuccessfully been used in attempts to support encroachments on the provincial legislative powers given by section 92. They laid down no principle of constitutional law, and were cautious words intended to safeguard possible eventualities which no one at the time had any interest or desire to define. The law of Canada on this branch of constitutional law has been stated with such force and clarity by the Chief Justice in his judgment in the reference concerning the Natural Products Marketing Act (93) dealing with the six acts there referred to, that their lordships abstained from stating it afresh. The Chief Justice, naturally from his point of view, excepted legislation to fulfil treaties. On this their lordships have expressed their opinion. But subject to this, they agree with and adopt what was there said. They consider that the law is finally settled by the current of cases cited by the Chief Justice on the principles declared by him.
It is only necessary to call attention to the phrases in the various cases, "abnormal circumstances", "exceptional conditions", "standard of necessity", (Board of Commerce case (94)), "seme extraordinary peril to the national life of Canada", "highly exceptional", "epidemic of pestilence", (Snider's case (95)), to show how far the present case is from the conditions which may override the normal distribution of powers in sections 91 and 92. The few pages of the chief justice's judgment will, it is to be hoped, form the locus classicus of the law on this point, and preclude further disputes." Their lordships think it sufficient to say, in answer to this third argument, that the prohibition now under consideration relates to civil rights within each of the provinces and that neither the facts set out in the order of reference, nor any other fact of which their lordships could take judicial notice, lead to the conclusion that there exists in the present case the conditions which may override the normal distribution of powers in sections 91 and 92.
May I say, Mr. Speaker, that if the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) feels I have not read sufficient of that judgment I shall be very pleased if he will extend the quotation.

But I would point out that this judgment has emphasized and re-emphasized that it is not only the safeguarding of the public interest that has to be borne in mind; that it is not merely a question of removing certain fetters upon free and equal competition, but that there must be some suggestion of a criminal aspect to the conduct which is under consideration. The judgments referred to with approval by the privy council have pointed out that where this principle has been supported it has not been under any loose doctrine that the parliament of Canada may declare anything to be criminal, but that it is something that relates to abnormal circumstances, exceptional conditions, that there is some great necessity, that there is extraordinary peril to the national life of Canada, that

Combines Investigation Act there is some epidemic or pestilence or something of that kind which must be dealt with.
These are the standards of emergency. These are the standards which are supposed to apply before this high court of parliament assumes the responsibility of declaring an act to be criminal. I am not presuming to place before this high court of parliament any dogmatic contention that the bill is necessarily ultra vires. Every lawyer who has been before our courts, every lawyer who has had such a wide experience in matters of this kind as the Prime Minister of Canada in his practice in earlier days, knows that even lawyers of the widest experience have on occasion found with surprise that the judges did not agree with the opinion they had originally expressed. I fancy that the Prime Minister, looking back over his years of experience, is not unique, and that he can perhaps recall cases where the court came to conclusions which were not entirely in line with the view he had originally expressed in regard to a subject of this kind. The fact that there is the possibility of such wide disagreement among highly trained legal minds is evidenced by the disagreement in the cases to which I have referred. I may say that not the present Prime Minister alone will recall that fact, because there is another member of this house who will recall, as a matter of family interest, the fact that there was a disagreement between the judges of the Supreme Court of Canada concerning the reference which had been placed before them on this subject.
There are great differences of opinion, and the balance sometimes goes one way and sometimes another. There are discernible trends in the judgments that are given. Sometimes one may detect a trend going on for a long time in one particular direction, and then the trend seems to go the other way. It may well be that at this time the trend of the judgments is to return to the original concept of confederation in which the rights conferred upon provincial legislatures were, in fact, to be exercised by provincial legislatures, and that the devices which were employed on so many occasions to override provincial jurisdiction should not be supported by the courts.
Believing as I do that the strength and unity of this country will depend upon a recognition of that distribution of power which was originally intended by those who drafted our federal constitution, I would hope that the tendency of our own Supreme Court of Canada would be in that direction. If it is, it may well be that the Supreme Court of Canada would hold that this subject matter now before us is the same subject

matter that was before the house at an earlier time when this house passed the Dominion Trade and Industry Commission Act, which included section 14 that was declared to be ultra vires because the subject matter of that section was beyond the jurisdiction of the parliament of Canada. I submit the court may well decide that if the subject matter was neither trade and commerce nor criminal law and it was not competent for parliament to pass that section with its permissive authority, then it is no more competent for this parliament to pass a section which follows a strictly negative course and places an overriding prohibition on all transactions of this nature.
Where is the criminal offence? We still have not been told. It has been suggested that this is not a desirable practice. It has been suggested by at least one member on the other side that this is something in the nature of a reaffirmation of historic Liberalism. I hope it is not the same kind of reaffirmation which the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier) placed before us when he introduced the amendments to the Public Works Act a few days ago. However, the Minister of Public Works must accept some responsibility for our pertinacity in continuing this debate, because we were successful in convincing him that it was desirable to change certain of the provisions in that bill. With that example before us, we still hope the government may recognize that there are reasons why this legislation should not be passed.
Mr. Speaker, we have not yet been told who the criminals are. There have been these statements about the friends of big business. I know there have been speeches about the desire to protect the manufacturer; but I recall that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) did#not give us examples of excessive profits by manufacturers. He gave us examples of what he regarded to be excessive write-ups between the price at which the manufacturer sold the article and the price at which the merchant sold it. I gather from this that he regards the merchant as the criminal in this case. Since that is the only thing he has put before us that by any stretch of the imagination can be suggested as supporting evidence for what he is doing, that is the only interpretation I can place upon it. I suggest that in so far as the responsibility of this high court of parliament is concerned, in declaring that this long established practice is in the nature of a criminal act we would be doing something very much like the communist government of east Germany did two days ago.

I was saying, Mr. Speaker,
that I was curious to know what opinion my hon. friend would entertain of section 498A of the Criminal Code which, as he will recall, was enacted by the Bennett government in 1935, if I remember rightly. The first part of that section reads as follows:
Every person engaged in trade or commerce or industry who
(a) is a party or privy to, or assists in, any transaction of sale which discriminates, to his knowledge, against competitors of the purchaser in that any discount, rebate or allowance is granted to the purchaser over and above any discount, rebate or allowance available at the time of such transaction to the aforesaid competitors in respect of a sale of goods of like quality and quantity-
-is guilty of an indictable offence, and so on. I suggest to my hon. friend, and I think upon reflection he will probably agree, that section 498A (a) which I have just read deals with a matter which but for section 498A (a) would be a commercial transaction lawfully within the power of those who took part in it. Thus that section, 498A, as my hon. friend himself has indicated, has

been the subject matter of a reference to determine its constitutionality. The case went before the Supreme Court of Canada, and the section was there held to be intra vires of parliament, with Justices Cannon and Crockett dissenting. Then it went from the Supreme Court of Canada to the privy council where it was held as reported in 1937, 1 Western Weekly Reports at page 319, and I quote this particularly because my hon. friend's quotation came to an abrupt stop at the very moment when he was beginning to get warm and come to the real point.

My hon. friend quoted this:
The only limitation on the plenary power of the dominion to determine what shall or shall not be criminal is the condition that parliament shall not in the guise of enacting criminal legislation in truth and in substance encroach on any of the classes of subjects enumerated in section 92.
That is, as coming within provincial jurisdiction. At that particular point my hon. friend came to an abrupt stop. The next sentence is this:
It is no objection that it does in fact affect them. If a genuine attempt to amend the criminal law, it may obviously affect previously existing civil rights. The object of an amendment-
And: I commend this particularly to my hon. friend.
The object of an amendment of the criminal law as a rule is to deprive the citizen of the right to do that which apart from the amendment he could lawfully do.
In other words, as applied to section 498A, here is a commercial transaction previously engaged in with perfect legality. Parliament comes along and by section 498A says: This much you previously did. You no longer can do it by reason of the enactment of this section.
Their Lordships go on further in their judgment to say this:
In the present case there seems to be no reason for supposing that the dominion are using the criminal law as a pretence or pretext or that the legislature is in pith and substance only interfering with civil rights in the province. Counsel for New Brunswick called the attention of the board to the report of the royal commission on price spreads, which is referred to in the order of reference. It probably would not be contended that the statement of the minister in the order of reference that the section was enacted to give effect to the recommendations of the royal commission bound the provinces or must necessarily be treated as conclusive by the board. But when the suggestion is made that the legislation was not in truth criminal legislation, but was in substance merely an encroachment on the provincial field, the existence of the report appears to be a material circumstance.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that there is this parallel between the constitutionality of section 498A of the Criminal Code and the validity of the legislation which is now before 94699-155
Combines Investigation Act us; that, as was referred to in this selection which I have just quoted, section 498A was preceded by a report of the royal commission on price spreads which was referred to in the order of reference, and that the legislation we have here covers the specific recommendations of the MacQuarrie committee. Therefore it would seem to the law officers of the crown that the constitutionality of section 37A, which is the operative portion of the present legislation, would appear to depend upon the same considerations that determined the constitutional validity of section 498A, and that there is not much doubt about it at all, certainly there is not sufficient doubt about it to warrant the course which is recommended in the present amendment before the house, namely, that we should go no further but should refer the matter to the courts to determine whether we are acting within the powers of parliament.
In the course of his discussion my hon. friend went on to say that he was somewhat disturbed by other cases which had been decided, notably the one dealing with section 14 of the Dominion Trade and Industry Commission Act. Perhaps the following selection from the judgment of Chief Justice Sir Lyman Duff might dispel some of the doubts that he entertained. Chief Justice Sir Lyman Duff said this:
As to section 14, we cannot perceive any ground for holding that the enactments of this section are necessarily incidental to the exercise of any powers of the dominion in relation to the criminal law. Nor can the section, we think, be sustained as legislation in relation to the regulation of trade and commerce consistently with the passage quoted from the judgment of the judicial committee in Snider's case (1), in the reasons given in the judgment upon the reference concerning the Natural Products Marketing Act. It is to be observed that this section contemplates action by the commission and by the governor in council in respect of individual agreements which may relate to trade that is entirely local.
That is not interprovincial or international trade, but trade wholly within a province. Then his lordship the chief justice goes on to say:
If confined to external trade and interprovincial trade, the section might well be competent under head No. 2 of section 91; and if the legislation were in substance concerned with such trade, incidental legislation in relation to local trade necessary in order to prevent the defeat of competent provisions might also be competent; but as it stands, we think this section is invalid.
Another case which apparently gave my hon. friend considerable mental anxiety, which he wishes to invoke as a basis for the amendment he has moved, was the judgment of the privy council in the margarine case. In that connection I should like to read some of the same selections from the privy council judgment that were read by my hon.

Combines Investigation Act friend; but, for some reason or other, I take a different meaning from them than he took.
The real point at issue in that case, I submit, was that in pith and substance, it was a law for the protection and encouragement of the dairy industry in Canada. And in the course of dealing with it their lordships of the privy council referred with approval to the judgment of Mr. Justice Rand, who had found that the object of the prohibition was economic, and the legislative purpose thereof was-and this is the nub of the matter, I suggest-to give trade protection to the dairy industry in the production and sale of butter. And then I quote from Mr. Justice Rand these words: "To benefit one group of persons as against competitors in business in which, in the absence of the legislation, the latter would be free to engage in the provinces." In other words it was distinguishing as between the civil rights of one group of people and the civil rights of another group of people. Again their lordships quote Mr. Justice Rand as follows:
"But to use it"-
And they are referring to the public interest in the regulation.
-"as a support lor the legislation in the aspect of criminal law would mean that the dominion under its authority in that field, by forbidding the manufacture or sale of particular products, could, in what it considered a sound trade policy, not only interdict a substantial part of the economic life of one section of Canada, but do so for the benefit of that of another."
And that is the point. Then their lordships again quote Mr. Justice Rand, and they are now referring, in the course of the discussion of this margarine case, to section 498A of the Criminal Code:
There the essential nature of the legislation was not the equalization of civil rights between competitors or promoting the interest of one grade as against another: it was the safeguarding of the public against the evil consequences of certain fetters upon free and equal competition.
I would like to know what the purpose of the legislation before this house is, if it is not the safeguarding of the public against the evil consequences of certain fetters upon free and equal competition, namely resale price maintenance.
And as their lordships went on to further quote Mr. Justice Rand in the margarine case:
There is no like purpose here; there is nothing of a general or injurious nature to be abolished or removed; it is a matter of preferring certain local trade to others.
In my view it was upon that basis that the legislation in question was held to be ultra vires. I might say therefore in conclusion that not a single principle my hon. 
friend has sought to establish in his lengthy	
remarks offers a	proper foundation for the
amendment he has moved.

I was paired with the hon. member for Chicoutimi (Mr. Gagnon). Had I voted, I would have voted against the amendment.
On motion of Mr. Chevrier the debate was adjourned.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Tomorrow we will proceed with this debate and then take up all other legislation. If the Secretary of State for External Affairs is here we will take up his resolution first.

At ten o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to the order of the house passed on November 2, 1951.
